title: The red squirrel
titleCn: 红松鼠摄影讲座：红松鼠与灰松鼠

paragraphs.text: Part two.
You will hear an amateur photographer called Darren giving a talk about his photographs of a type of animal called a squirrel.
First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fifteen.
Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fifteen.
Thanks for inviting me here today.

I'll start by showing you some of my photographs and explaining a bit of background about the red squirrel, and then give some general advice for those of you who might be interested in doing some nature photography of your own.
So let's look at my first slide, a young red squirrel. Its Latin name, Sciurus vulgaris, derives from the Greek word scia, meaning shadow, and ura, meaning tail.

I thought this was a bit funny at first and couldn't make any sense of the phrase until I realized that it translated as an animal sitting in the shadow of its tail. And then it all fell into place because that's what the red squirrel does. This photo was taken right outside my back door.
Before I started, I set myself the goal of taking all these photographs in my garden, but using different kinds of camera and incorporating a variety of different contextual features.
Squirrels amongst birds, for example.
But why such a fascination with this animal?

Well, the red squirrel was once common throughout much of Britain. In the late nineteenth century, the American gray squirrel was introduced into this country. Some people believe that they brought a disease with them that reduced the red squirrel population. But the decline of the red species had already started long before the grays came to the country, and my theory is that it's to do with fewer nuts, which reds love to eat, being available.
The only place reds seem to thrive now is in one or two ancient forests.
But how did I go about capturing them on film?
Well, a wildlife photographer friend of mine advised me to use lure or bait of hazelnuts.
She told me that you have to attract them over several months by leaving out nuts.
Of course, lots of other animals love to eat hazelnuts, but evidence of red squirrels is clear.
Mice, for example, gnaw a neat hole through the shell, whereas a red squirrel picks up the nut, spins it until it finds a fault line, and splits it in two with one bite, removing the nut from within.
I soon began to see signs of red squirrel visits to my patch, and I knew that I'd eventually see the animals themselves.
I was amazed by how soon they started arriving, jumping delightfully around the trees and clotheslines.

At first, they were very reluctant to come within a ten-meter radius of me, but soon they began to recognize the hand that fed them, and they boldly approached me. And I began to get some pretty remarkable photographs.

It's curious, but the actual photography side of things didn't bother me too much. Although I had had only a little practice and my cameras were largely secondhand, I'd had a very good mentor and picked up a lot of tips from her.
It was really the attracting of the animals and capturing them in the most natural situations that I was most concerned about.
Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.
Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.
I exhibited a selection of them in the local museum when friends advised me to show them to a wider audience.
Also, much to my surprise, I won third prize in a competition organized by a national newspaper.
But what advice can I give to any of you who might be thinking of embarking on something similar?
Well, Tracy, my photography expert friend, and I spent a bit of time thinking about this, and we came up with the following five points specifically related to nature photography.
First of all, although a good camera is always of great importance, the crucial requirement for this kind of work must be a tripod.
The level of detail needed, not to mention the weight of a good zoom lens, means that simply bracing your arm won't do.
Next, our review of a large number of outstanding photographs tells us that just having the animal in shot can be misleading.

Make sure you set up the shot in such a way that what is named a secondary object is in view. It can be a branch, flowers, masonry, whatever you want. This helps portray the prime object in proper perspective. Next, and this might seem bizarre, take care to look behind you when you're setting up a shot.
The number of times I've found that the most original new shot is in the very place I've just passed.
Now, it's a well-known dictum in photography that midday or early afternoon light has the effect of bleaching true color. Late afternoon light is my favorite, with its warm red colors.
Morning light can be beautiful but has a starker yellow glow.
And finally, if you are at all serious about your nature or wildlife photography, take the trouble to make detailed notes on all your shots.
Mention information on time, equipment, setting, etc., and this will work like a recipe book to help you recognize what contributed to successful shots.
That is the end of part two. You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part two.
